title: Injection through query construction and dataflow gaps
summary: SQL and comparable query injection becomes plausible when untrusted data reaches a query, command, or template that the interpreter parses as structure rather than as a value. Verification must follow the real dataflow to the sink, establish whether the value is bound as a parameter or concatenated into the statement, identify the interpreter that actually parses it, and demonstrate a bounded change in query structure rather than assuming that any dynamic string is exploitable.
detection_signals: Request, queue, file, or third-party data reaches a query builder, raw execution helper, stored procedure argument, or ORM escape hatch that accepts a statement fragment.
Identifiers that cannot be bound as parameters, such as table names, column names, sort keys, or direction tokens, are interpolated from request data instead of mapped from a fixed set.
Escaping, encoding, or sanitization is applied in a different layer, character set, or order than the interpreter that finally parses the statement.
safe_local_tests: Exercise the sink against a disposable local database seeded with fixture rows, and assert on the statement the driver actually issues rather than on the rendered page alone.

Prove structure change with a benign, non-destructive payload such as a tautology or an added ordering term, and never run destructive, timing-abusive, or data-exfiltrating payloads on shared systems.
Record the source parameter, the executed statement text, the bound parameter list, and the resulting row set as the dataflow evidence for the finding.
false_positive_traps: String concatenation is not proof when the concatenated value is a server-generated constant, an enum already validated against an allowlist, or a value the driver still binds as a parameter.
A database error message is evidence of parsing, not of an exploitable structure change, and error-based signals can also come from type coercion or a driver-level rejection.
A grep hit on a raw query helper may sit behind an unreachable role, a disabled feature flag, or a migration path that never receives untrusted input.
remediation_patterns: Bind every value through parameterized queries, prepared statements, or the ORM's typed API, and treat any remaining concatenation as an exception that needs a documented justification.
Map non-bindable identifiers such as sort columns and table names through a server-side allowlist that translates a request token into a fixed, code-owned identifier.
Keep validation, encoding, and the executing interpreter aligned in one layer, and give the application's database account only the privileges the feature needs so a residual defect stays bounded.
regression_proof: A test replays the exact payload that previously changed query structure and asserts that it is now treated as a literal value with an unchanged statement shape.
Coverage includes the non-bindable identifier paths, nested and batch queries, and a negative case proving that legitimate values with quotes or comment characters still work.
